root.text: I have a customer that is asking about claude.md support, I am thinking about responding with the following, as I am still learning the nuances of Atlas I need some assistance to vet the following: CLAUDE.md as a file format — no, Atlas does not support it. That's an Anthropic-specific convention where you drop a markdown file into a repo and Claude reads it as persistent instructions. But that's not a workaround situation — it's an architectural difference worth explaining clearly. ☆ Why CLAUDE.md Exists and What It Actually Does CLAUDE.md is a developer convenience pattern — it injects static context/instructions into Claude's system prompt at the start of every session. It's essentially a text file that becomes part of the prompt. It works because Claude is trained to recognize and follow it. The limitation: it's model-dependent, prompt-dependent, and unenforced. The model can still ignore it, be manipulated past it, or have it overridden by a sufficiently clever prompt injection. ☆ What Atlas Does Instead — and Why It's Stronger Atlas doesn't inject instructions into the model — it governs around the model at the infrastructure level. The distinction matters: CLAUDE.md Atlas Policy Where it lives Inside the prompt Outside the model — infrastructure layer Enforcement Model-dependent (can be ignored/bypassed) Hard enforcement — block/modify before model ever sees it Scope Claude only Any LLM — Claude, Gemini, GPT, WatsonX, custom models Auditability None Full policy change history, staging/review workflow Model can bypass it? Yes No — guardrails fire regardless of model behavior ☆ The Closest Direct Equivalent in Atlas If what Camelot wants is "persistent instructions that shape AI behavior across all sessions" — the Atlas equivalent is: Custom Judge — Natural language criteria evaluated by a separate LLM judge at runtime. Write it exactly like a CLAUDE.md instruction set. Unlike CLAUDE.md, the target model never even sees it — it runs independently. Policy Message Rule — Prepends or appends a fixed instruction/context block to every prompt or response automatically. This is the most direct structural equivalent to what CLAUDE.md does — except it's enforced at the proxy level, not the model level. Banned Substrings + Prompt Protection Rules — For specific behavioral boundaries that CLAUDE.md would normally define (don't discuss X, never output Y). ☆ The Bottom Line for the Room Don't frame this as a workaround. Atlas doesn't support CLAUDE.md because it doesn't need to — it enforces behavior at a layer the model can't override. For a cybersecurity company like Camelot whose clients need to trust that AI guardrails hold, "the model follows instructions in a text file" is a weaker guarantee than "the infrastructure blocks it regardless of what the model does."

root.text: Elio Gerardi Matt Proctor Q. So I have a question about Shadow AI. A customer is asking how do they make sure that everyone is using the AI GAteway for Real Time protection. What stops a user from going around that? IS it just networking they need to ensure that everything gets routed through their Firewalls and then to the AI GAteway? This question comes up re: ensuring developers and users are not bypassing the gateway/runtime, and you are indeed kind of starting to answer your own question there. Alot of times this comes down to a customer already having their own API Gateway or network infrastructure in place. In the past a few of the integration options that we've seen customers explore on implementation are: Direct Firewall API Callouts - this method involves configuring the customer's own API Gateway to directly call the Atlas firewall APIs. The customer's own API Gateway must support some sort of Request API callout function, similar to what the Kong service offers (this essentially duplicates what our own proxy does) Proxy Chaining - the customer routes their traffic through their own API Gateway, which then forwards the request to the Atlas proxy, and finally to the LLM Endpoint. The main consideration for the customer is that it involves going through two proxies. SDK Integration with API Gateway Checks - this option involves deploying the Atlas SDK directly within the customer's applications. The customer's API Gateway can then be used to check the quarantine or approval status of an endpoint. The main consideration for the customer is ensuring that the SDK has been deployed properly. All of these options are possible, and the choice depends on what makes the most sense for a given implementation. Generally speaking, on more advanced implementations we will get our best together with their best and engineer a solution. These scenarios aren't one-size-fits-all but we can get creative. To quote Chris Prangley - just say yes, we can support this in a few different ways. Somebody like Abdiel or other members of the team that are of a higher level than me may have additional insights. I hope this helps.

root.text: Q: Are the AI Usage, MCP, Investigation, and TPRM menus directly tied to specific SKUs, or do later SKUs enrich what is already visible? A: AI Usage is Part of SKU 1. Investigation is part of SKU 2 (SKU 1 features + runtime/guardrails/monitoring). TPRM is part of SKU 3 (SKU's 1 and 2 + compliance features)

root.author: Unknown
root.text: Q: How do we identify excessive tools or excessive agency? Is this based on configuration review, runtime observation, or something else? A: Agentic Risk is part of AI SPM, which analyzes the configuration of the discovered asset to analyze the risk. This does not require runtime observation, and thus is available with SKU 1. Note: Additional agentic-related risks, like Shadow MCP server risks, are detected at runtime as we cannot see what tools an external MCP server has access to until they are called. This correlates to the new 'AI MCP' section of the UI.
